en: The *Record of Miraculous Responses to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (Dafangguangfo Huayanjing Ganyingzhuan),
compiled and edited by the lay practitioner Hu Youzhen of Mount Siming, the Great Avataṃsaka [Society].
This record was collected by the monk Huiying, a disciple of the Venerable Master Zang, the commentator on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The work originally consisted of two volumes, upper and lower.
Now, I find its external rhetoric shallow and its expressions regarding auspicious responses verbose;
therefore, I have edited and condensed it into a single volume.
May those who have seen or heard this secret vehicle conceive the thought that it is difficult to encounter,
and may each of you strive to uphold and maintain it.
In the Western Regions, there was the Bodhisattva Asaṅga, whose younger brother was Vasubandhu.
In his youth, he studied the inner teachings;
in his maturity, he mastered the five divisions of the Abhidharma.
Initially, he practiced the Hinayana and composed five hundred treatises on the Hinayana. Asanga,
pitying his intellectual brilliance yet lack of aspiration for the Mahayana, [intervened].
Deeply enamored with the minor teachings, he disparaged the Great Vehicle.
He then feigned illness as a skillful means,
sending someone to summon him and entice him forward.
He extensively explained for him the causes and karmic conditions of illness;
thereupon, Vasubandhu took up the *Vimalakīrti*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, *Avataṃsaka*, and other sūtras that his elder brother had mastered,
reciting them aloud.
Asanga listened with rapt attention,
feeling both joy and sorrow; Vasubandhu,
however, had already perused the sutra for several days.
Only then did he attain faith and awakening,
and came to deeply revere the One Vehicle of the Avataṃsaka as the realm of all Buddhas.
He then abandoned his minor teacher for the major one,
deeply repenting his faults;
wishing to sever his own tongue with a sharp blade as an atonement for his past transgressions.
Asanga admonished him, saying: "Previously,
you used your mouth to promote provisional teachings and to disparage and reject the True Vehicle."
Now, by using your own mouth to praise the True Vehicle,
you shall extinguish your own deep karmic burdens.
"What is the use of cutting out my tongue?
Vasubandhu then entered the mountains to receive and uphold the *Avataṃsaka*.
Later, while composing the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*,
he encountered points that were not fully understood;
he came to ask Maitreya about them.
Asaṅga had not yet attained full realization;
he ascended to the Tuṣita Heaven to seek instructions from Maitreya.
As soon as the treatise was finished,
the earth shook violently,
and the treatise emitted a brilliant light.
It illuminated several hundred *li*,
and the entire nation celebrated this miraculous event,
as described in detail in the *Biography of Wuzhuo*.
During the Wei dynasty, the monk Lingbian of Bingzhou left home as a youth and applied his mind with devotion to the Buddha-vehicle.
He specialized exclusively in the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra.
At that time, no commentaries or treatises existed;
he constantly contemplated its profound meaning, yet had nowhere to seek instruction.
Thereupon, he adorned the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and wore the *Avataṃsaka* upon his head;
he practiced the Way day and night for six years.
With blood flowing at every step,
he entreated Mañjuśrī with grief for the Buddha’s empowerment,
vowing to master the profound scriptures.
His sincerity remained unswerving;
suddenly, one night, he was moved by a vision of a youthful deity.
Upon attaining clear and lucid awakening to the dharmadhātu of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra through its seven locations and nine assemblies,
he immediately entered a subtle meditative concentration as if it were that very moment.
It was as if I had personally witnessed it with my eyes, heard it with my ears, and grasped it with my mind;
what I had not previously understood,
I now comprehend without exception.
He subsequently composed the *Huayan lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka) in one hundred fascicles at Mount Xiong in Xian County, on that continent.
[This was done by] the Eastern Jin śramaṇa Zhi Falin.
He left home to become a monk in his youth.
His mental conduct was diligent and his resolve firm;
he lamented that after the passing of the Muni, the True Teaching had declined and fallen into decay.
He then traveled to the Western Heaven to seek out the sacred scriptures.
Upon reaching Khotan,
he suddenly encountered the Tripiṭaka Master of the One Vehicle, Buddhabhadra, who had come from the West.
He was known as Jñānabhadra.
He was a descendant of King Amṛtodana of the Śākya clan and was a person who had attained the third fruit of the Mahāyāna path.
He was then a Bodhisattva of the Third Ground.
He brought the Sanskrit original of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, consisting of more than thirty-six thousand verses.
If there were any points in the scripture that were not understood, [he would resolve them].
He immediately ascended to Tuṣita Heaven and questioned the World-Honored One Maitreya,
requesting that Dharmapāla compassionately descend to China to circulate the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
Having come to the capital at the request [of the Emperor], he settled there;
his conduct and posture were not like those of ordinary people,
sometimes even within the windows.
He moved in and out without obstruction,
leaving all the monks living with him utterly amazed and astonished.
Everyone called him a demon.
The assembly of monks then asked the Tripiṭaka Master,
"Has the Dharma Master attained the state of a superhuman?"
The Tripitaka Master replied,
"I have now attained it. Thereupon,
the various masters assembled the monastic community in the capital city.
While he was performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) with the intent to expel him,
the Tripitaka Master then took up his robes and bowl and ascended into the air.
Manifesting various supernatural transformations,
he leaped up from his seat and flew south toward Jambudvīpa,
soaring through the sky like a bird.
The assembled monks were struck with dismay and regret;
it was impossible to turn back.
On the fourteenth day of the third month in the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, he passed away.
At Xie Sijing Temple in Jianye,
he constructed the Hujing Dharma Hall and translated the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
While the sutras were being translated,
a pond suddenly manifested before the hall.
Every morning at dawn, two youths dressed in green appeared.
Emerging from the pond,
he swept and cleaned the sutra hall,
ground ink, and attended to his master.
At dusk, he returned to stay overnight in the pond.
It is traditionally said that the Śākya explained:
"This sutra has long resided in the Dragon Palace."
Because the Dragon King rejoiced in this translation,
he personally attended to him;
later, this monastery was renamed Xingyan Monastery.
The śramaṇas Huìyè, Huìyán, Huìguān, and others acted as scribes for the Tripiṭaka Master, while Mèng Yǐ,
the Prefect of Hào Commandery, served as the patron.
The Right Guard General Zhū Shūdù and others served as patrons (*dānapati*).
The translation was completed on the tenth day of the sixth month in the second year of the Yuánxī era.
Later, on the twentieth day of the twelfth month in the second year of the Yǒngchū era of the Dàzōng period.
After it had been collated once more with the Sanskrit original,
the Song Emperor requested that the Tripiṭaka Master Nāgabodhi lecture on this sūtra.
The Tripiṭaka Master regretted that his mastery of the local dialect was not yet sufficient.
Failing to fully grasp the purport of the sutra,
he entered the dharma hall and requested that Avalokiteśvara be invoked;
before seven days had passed, [the response was realized].
He subsequently dreamed that his Han head was replaced by a Brahmanical head;
consequently, he immediately attained profound understanding of the Qin language.
He is the one known at the time as the "Head-Exchanged Tripiṭaka Master."
When the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra first arrived in Guanzhong,
he asked Dharma Master Kumārajīva:
"What are the sutras and treatises you have translated?
Kumārajīva replied,
"The Lotus Sutra, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra, and others."
Regarding the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* and other treatises,
the Tripiṭaka Master said:
"As you have translated them."
He had not yet emerged from among the ranks of ordinary men;
how could he be worthy of such a grand reputation?
At that time, the Tripitaka Master was highly acclaimed throughout Guanzhong.
He was a great master of treatises.
On another day, Yao Xing, the ruler of Qin,
invited the Tripiṭaka Master to the Eastern Palace to engage in debate.
There were more than three thousand scholars seated below him,
including the Buddhists Dao-sheng, Seng-zhao, Tan-rong,
and Zhi-yi, and the Confucians Xie Lingyun and Fei Changfang.
No one dared to raise a question;
Master Shi then raised his voice and asked,
"What do you consider to be right view?"
The Tripitaka Master said,
"It means seeing that all dharmas are empty.
Kumārajīva said:
"Since it is empty, what is there to be seen?
He replied, "I see emptiness; this cannot be called 'not seeing'."
Kumārajīva asked,
"Can emptiness be seen?
The Tripiṭaka Master replied, "No."
"Emptiness cannot be seen.
Kumārajīva asked again,
"How do you refute the emptiness of form?"
The Tripitaka Master said:
"Form has no intrinsic nature;
it is formed by the aggregation of many atoms."
The transformation of form is extremely subtle; this is why form is empty.
Kumārajīva said:
"You have already rendered color empty by means of the most minute particles;
how then can you further refute the emptiness of those ultimate particles?
The Tripitaka Master replied:
Everyone divides [space] by means of its spatial dimensions,
asserting that the ultimate atom (paramāṇu) is empty.
In my view, this is not so.
Śrī said, "What do you think?
Tripiṭaka replied:
Because of one atom there are many atoms;
because of many atoms there is one atom.
Atoms have no intrinsic nature.
"What is there to refute?
When Master Kumārajīva heard this,
he was utterly bewildered and did not know what kind of discourse this was.
Consequently, he no longer questioned him further.
At that time, none among the assembly could fathom the profound purport of the Tripiṭaka and the One Vehicle.
Furthermore, as they followed and supported Master Kumārajīva, it was said:
The Tripitaka Master had no answer,
whereupon the discussion was brought to a close.
Once the Tripitaka Master had returned to his monastery, he—
Daosheng, Sengzhao, Baoyun,
and others went to him again to inquire about resolving their previous doubts, saying,
"Master Kumārajīva does not yet understand what you are discussing."
The Tripitaka Master said,
"This meaning is difficult to comprehend;
my words are very easy."
Kumārajīva himself was utterly bewildered.
Later, Kumārajīva again questioned him as before,
but in the end, no one could fathom the answer.
Youzhen asked: "This commentary by Master Shi (Kumārajīva) is recorded as belonging to the One Vehicle.
What is the meaning of 'a śramaṇa whose form is the Way'?"
Because we desire to together examine the treatises on the One Vehicle and jointly hear the teachings of the Tripitaka,
we have appended this [work] herein.
Dharma Master Huiju of the Northern Qi dynasty felt weary of worldly life from his youth; as an adult,
he devoted himself to the study of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
For fifteen or sixteen years,
within the site of enlightenment, he performed circumambulations while prostrating during the six periods of the day.
He recited and maintained [the mantra] day and night without the slightest weariness; then,
within a dream during sleep, he saw a young boy.
Calling himself Shancai,
he said to Huiju, "Since you,
Master, are already able to study the *Sūtra of the Flower Ornament*,..."
Desiring to investigate the realm of the Buddha,
he came southward the following day and gave the Master the "Medicine of Intelligence."
He caused his teacher to realize the essential meaning of the sutra.
At dawn the next day, Huìjù presented this matter in detail to the assembly of monks,
whereupon they performed a ritual bath with fragrant water.
Clad in pure garments and holding an incense burner in hand,
take refuge in the Triple Gem.
"May that which I seek be obtained as surely as in a dream. Having said this,
he immediately traveled south with the youth.
With mind and mouth focused single-mindedly,
he constantly kept Mañjuśrī in his thoughts for several li along the way.
Suddenly he saw a pond,
half a li in circumference,
with various flowers surrounding its banks and calamus growing there.
The Acorus calamus is a medicine for sharpening the intellect;
therefore, he commanded his young attendants to enter the water to gather it.
Suddenly, they obtained a single root as large as a chariot axle.
He returned to the temple and swallowed a dose about the size of a jujube;
immediately he felt lightened and his spirit became refreshed.
He recited ten thousand words daily and thereby attained a profound understanding of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
composing more than ten fascicles of commentary on this scripture.
He lectured on the sutra fifty times.
During the Yongwei era of the Great Tang,
there was a lay practitioner named Xuanzhi.
A fellow student of Master Huayan Zang,
he entered the Way in his early twenties;
he attained mastery in the Five Classics, the Tripitaka, and the inner teachings of Buddhism.
He specialized exclusively in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra and resided on Mount Fangzhou;
initially, he subsisted on pine needles.
For over sixty years, he recited and upheld [the scriptures] without fail. Fifty years ago,
he was moved by the earth to gush forth sweet spring water at his dwelling place.
The offerings were more than sufficient;
the grove produced exquisite fruits,
with every tree laden with abundant fruit.
People from far and near gathered [the wood],
without any hindrance;
suddenly, deep snow began to fall.
Provisions could not be transported, and his store of food for the fast was gradually exhausted;
at that point, there appeared a mountain deity.
The appearance of the sent medicine resembles clarified butter (ghṛta),
and its taste is sweeter than milk;
it is enough to take a single dose.
For seven days he was not hungry;
his mental and physical strength increased further,
his body became light, and his vision grew clear.
If one performs prostrations and recitations at night,
lamps will appear spontaneously;
if one recites the sutras during the day, [the same occurs].
Then the flocks of birds gathered to listen,
and the retinue of mountain deities manifested their forms and surrounded him.
Exquisite fragrances would occasionally waft forth,
and wondrous fruits arrived from time to time;
sometimes he would recite the scriptures at night.
Light issued from his mouth,
illuminating an area of more than forty li;
the color of the light was like gold.
People from both far and near were struck with wonder.
Some went to search for him at the mountain,
where they saw only the lay practitioner reciting a sutra, with light radiating from his mouth.
At that time, he was ninety-two years old and passed away without illness.
At the time of his cremation:
The teeth were transformed into śarīras;
more than a hundred grains were obtained,
all of which emitted radiant light.
It did not cease for several days.
At that time, both monastics and laypeople collected it and erected a stupa to make offerings to it.
During the Yonghui era,
there were two monks at Chanding Monastery named Daoxiang and Huiwu.
Both concealed themselves within the Taibai Mountains;
Xiang recited the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
while Wu recited the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
He consumed pine needles and wild rice;
he performed prostrations and repentance during the six periods of the day and night; and he recited and maintained [the scriptures] day and night.
Many years had passed when,
on one occasion, he suddenly saw a layman with hair as white as snow.
Her garments were pure white;
her appearance was grand and beautiful.
She came forward and performed a ritual prostration.
Speaking with decorum,
I have established a vegetarian feast at my humble residence and wish to invite a monk.
The monk said,
"There are only two monks here;
would it not be acceptable for both of us to go together?"
The layman said,
"I am but a poor man; originally,
I intended to invite only one monk."
A monk asked, "Whom do you intend to invite? He replied, "I have invited the Dharma Master of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
Wuzhuo then went to accept the invitation.
He followed the householder for about a hundred paces.
At that point, the householder...
Leaping into the air, Teng asked Wu,
"Why does the Master not ascend into the sky? Wu replied:
"I, a poor monk, have no wings;
I have not yet attained the ability to ascend into the sky.
Layman, ask about my awakening."
"Has the Master still not attained supernatural powers?
Wù replied, "In truth, I have not yet attained them."
The layman descended from the air and sat upon the lap of the layman Anzhiwu;
he then commanded him to close his eyes.
At that time, he heard only the whistling sound of the wind by his ears for about half the duration of a meal; then,
he placed his sandals back upon the ground.
He then ordered his eyes to be opened;
not knowing where he had arrived,
he looked all around and saw only a great mountain.
He observed that the buildings were all emerging from the earth;
he then led Wuru into the hall.
As soon as he had finished paying homage to the Buddha,
he suddenly saw five hundred extraordinary monks,
holding mendicant staffs and carrying alms bowls.
He arrived flying through the air; Daowu,
recognizing him as a monk of extraordinary virtue,
did not dare to sit above him.
He then followed him down.
When the lay devotee arrived, he said to him,
"Master, you have received and upheld the Avataṃsaka Sūtra."
"This is the realm of the Buddha.
How could he take a seat below that of the Lesser Sages?
Thus, he subsequently led them to awakening."
He sat at the head of five hundred holy beings.
After the meal, once they had washed and rinsed their mouths,
the holy ones ascended into the air and departed.
The lay devotee then sent someone carrying a bed of precious objects to present as a gift to Bodhidharma,
requesting that he perform a ritual of blessing for them.
Wu said, "I,
this poor monk, did not come here by my own power;
it was the Layman who led me here."
I am unable to return on my own;
I beg you to escort me back so that I may recite the scriptures to repay your kindness.
The lay devotee said,
"My original intention for this vegetarian feast was solely for you, Master.
Even if five hundred arhats were to come to eat, [it would still be for you alone]."
"We have all been invited on this occasion.
Please bestow upon us a prayer for blessings,
and we shall immediately dispatch someone."
Having escorted him back to his original residence and completed the awakening and the incantation,
there were three or five youths standing before him.
Each was about six or seven years old.
When the householder called them,
one boy in particular came forward immediately as his name was called out once more.
The layman said, "You should serve this Dharma Master. Thereupon,
the youth requested of Awu (Wù), saying:
The Master opened his mouth for a moment;
Wù immediately followed the opening.
The youth observed this and said:
The Master was very ill;
the youth then took his hand and rubbed it over the Master's body.
He then took a small amount of medicine,
about the size of a sesame seed,
and divided it into three pills.
Wu swallowed it, and when he was asked to open his mouth again,
the youth suddenly flew into his mouth.
Upon awakening, he immediately ascended into the void and returned to his original dwelling;
standing in mid-air, he said to Xiang:
Having recently received an invitation to a vegetarian feast from the Immortal Layman,
I have attained supernatural powers.
I now wish to travel briefly to the palaces of Penglai, the Golden Gate, and Ziwai.
Having recited his fundamental practice and finished his auspicious words of departure,
he gathered his three robes, water flask, alms bowl, and the scriptures he had received.
He ascended into the air and departed.
This occurred during the Qianqing era.
On Mount Jiulung there was a nun whose resolve was refined in the Buddha-vehicle and the secret treasury of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra;
she entered the mountains to receive and uphold it.
For over twenty years,
he performed rituals and recitations without fail,
practicing in accordance with the teachings.
With his nature stabilized and his mind tranquil,
he subsequently realized the eye of wisdom and attained the realm of Indra’s net.
The oceans of lands as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions and the sites of enlightenment for the nine assemblies were clearly perceived,
appearing like reflections in a mirror.
In the first year of the Zongzhang era,
three Tripitaka masters from the Western Regions arrived at the capital of Luoyang.
Emperor Gaozong served him as his teacher;
both monastics and laypeople turned to him with reverence. Master Huayan Fazang—
Still acting as a youth,
he prostrated before the Tripitaka Master and requested to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
At that time, the assembly said to the Tripitaka Master:
"This youth has mastered the recitation of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra and also understands its meaning."
The Tripitaka Master marveled and said,
"The One Vehicle of the Avataṃsaka is the secret treasury of all Buddhas;
it is difficult to encounter."
How much more so for one who masters its meaning!
If there is anyone who can recite the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
that person has already attained the full perfection of the Bodhisattva's pure precepts.
One does not receive the bodhisattva precepts again.
In the biographies of the Western Regions,
it is said that there was a person who recited the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
Using water for washing his hands,
he let a drop fall upon an ant;
the ant’s life came to an end.
One is reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
how much more so for a person who is able to receive and uphold it—
one should know that such a person is a true youth.
In the future, it will surely bring vast benefit and be able to bestow upon all living beings the nectar of non-arising.
During the Shangyuan era.
There was a monk at Jing’ai Temple in Luozhou whose place of origin was Zhengzhou;
he had returned there to pay his respects to his relatives.
He traveled to the borders of Zhengzhou and stayed overnight at an inn.
There, another monk arrived.
Not knowing his name,
he also stayed overnight at an inn with the monk who had arrived earlier.
They were placed side by side.
Later, a visiting monk said to the host,
"I have come from afar."
Exhausted, weary, and famished,
the host bought three sheng of wine and purchased one jin of meat.
He possesses the necessary funds;
please deliver them to him with all speed, without delay.
The host immediately prepared it as requested.
The monk ate it all.
This was the Venerable Jingai.
He became enraged and rebuked him,
saying: "Clad in the dharma robes,
you eat wine and meat at will before laypeople."
Lacking a sense of shame or remorse,
the monk remained silent and gave no reply until the first watch of the night.
He drew water to rinse his mouth,
sat upright in the full-lotus posture,
and began to chant in the Brahma-voice.
Recite the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*:
first, state the title of the chapter;
next, recite: "Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying in the country of Magadha, at the site of enlightenment (Śītavane Mṛgadāve)."
On both corners of that monk’s mouth,
light radiated forth,
appearing like the color of gold.
Those who heard it shed tears;
those who saw it gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment;
even the Vinaya Master was filled with admiration.
I privately reflected to myself:
"Those monks who consume wine and meat are yet able to recite this great sutra."
By the third watch,
the sound of the recitation was still heard without ceasing;
the fourth volume was nearly finished.
The light from his mouth became even more intensely blazing,
pervading the entire universe.
The light permeated through the pores and illuminated both chambers;
at first, the Vinaya Master did not recognize it as light and said:
"Why does that guest not extinguish the lamp?
He is wasting the host's oil.
For this reason, the Vinaya Master established the method for rising to go to the toilet.
He caught sight of golden light emerging from the two corners of the monk’s mouth;
when he had recited more than five fascicles,
the light gradually withdrew.
He then returned it to the mouths of the monks;
at the fifth watch of the night, he finished reciting six sets of the scriptures,
whereupon the monks lay down to sleep.
In a brief moment, dawn broke.
The Vinaya Master wept and approached,
prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground.
I seek mercy and repent for my transgressions;
having lightly slandered the worthy and the holy,
I pray that my offenses may be extinguished.
During the Yifeng era,
two Brahman monks from the Western Regions arrived at Mount Wutai.
Carrying a lotus flower and holding an incense burner,
he moved on his elbows and knees toward the mountain peak to pay homage to the Great Sage Mañjuśrī.
He encountered a nun among the rocky cliffs beneath a pine tree,
sitting upright and alone upon a rope bed, reciting the Avataṃsaka Sūtra;
at that time, the daylight was already fading.
The nun said to the bhikṣu,
"It is not permissible for a nun to stay overnight with the great saṃgha of monks.
Venerable sir, please depart."
"Come again tomorrow.
The monk said,
"The mountain road is deep and far."
"Having nowhere else to turn,
I pray that you will not send me away.
The nun said:
"Unless you leave, I cannot remain here;
I must enter the deep mountains.
The monk paced back and forth, filled with shame and trepidation.
"I do not know where it has gone," [the monk] said.
The nun replied,
"Just descend to the lower valley."
There was a meditation cave there where monks resided;
going to search for it, he eventually found the meditation cave.
The distance between them was about five li or more.
Two monks, with single-minded devotion, joined their palms and held incense burners in their hands.
Facing north, he paid distant homage;
with his whole heart, he listened to the sutra,
hearing it clearly in his ears.
At the very beginning of opening the scripture’s title,
it says, "Thus have I heard," whereupon he saw that nun from afar.
He sat upon a corded couch facing south,
emitting light from his mouth.
Brilliant like the color of gold,
it shone clearly upon the front peak.
Having recited more than two fascicles of the sutras, [he continued].
The radiance was so intense south of the valley that it extended for ten li in both width and circumference;
it was no different from daylight.
The sutra consists of forty fascicles.
The light gradually withdrew;
when the sixth fascicle was completed,
the light entered the nun’s mouth entirely.
The "Bodhisattva Abodes" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"In the northeastern direction of the land of China, there is a bodhisattva abode named Mount Qingliang."
All bodhisattvas of the past have always dwelt therein;
so too do the bodhisattvas of the present.
He is named Mañjuśrī.
Accompanied by ten thousand bodhisattvas,
his mountain is located on the northeastern bend of the Southern Zhai Continent.
It is named Mount Wutai.
The *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* states:
"Mañjuśrī was, in the past, the Buddha Dragon-Species Supreme Honored King (*Nāgottara-rāja*) in the world of Equality."
Furthermore, the *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"Mañjuśrī is the Maṇiratnarāśi Buddha of the world of Joy (*Ratiprabhā*) in the eastern direction;
that is the domain of that goddess."
This must have been a manifestation of Mañjuśrī’s transformative power,
displayed for the sake of the Indian monk.
This was at the beginning of the Chuigong era.
There was the Tripitaka Master of Central India, Sūryavarman,
who traveled from afar bringing Sanskrit scriptures to this land for translation.
Emperor Gaozong issued an edict to station him at Taoyuan Monastery.
He summoned the great virtuous monks of the capital to jointly translate more than ten sutras, including the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Ghanavyūha*.
The monks Daocheng, Bocen, Yuanze, Yìng, and others served as witnesses to the meaning.
Fulei, Sisi, and others took up their pens;
Hui and Zhi and others served as translators.
At that time, Master Huayan Zang was at the monastery.
During the course of the translation, he asked the Tripitaka Master:
"In the Western Regions, have there been any who, by upholding the One Vehicle, attained spiritual responses?
The Tripitaka Master replied:
Recently, while seeking a teacher,
I arrived at a temple in the southern heavens during the night;
